title: We the People: Representation and Ratification, 1787–1791

sheetTitle.es: Nosotros, el pueblo: representación y ratificación, 1787–1791

summary: See how House seats were shared out after the 1790 census, how the three-fifths clause changed the count, and how close each state's vote to ratify was.
subject: History
studentLogin: Not needed to explore the map

layers.name: Population in 1790: free and enslaved
layers.shows: A pie on each state: free people (blue) and enslaved people (orange-red) in the 1790 census, with bigger pies for more people. Each pop-up, titled with the state's name, gives the total, the number enslaved and the percentage, the number counted under the three-fifths clause, the state's House seats in 1793, its two senators, and the seats it would have had if enslaved people had been counted in full or not at all.
layers.source: 1790 census figures as tabulated on Wikipedia, checked against the 1793 House seats; seats from the National Archives; ratio from the U.S. Census Bureau; state outlines from Natural Earth

layers.name: House seats in 1793
layers.shows: States shaded from pale to dark blue by their House seats under the apportionment act of 14 April 1792 (legend: 1 to 2, 4 to 6, 7 to 10, 13 to 19 seats), labeled with the state's abbreviation and seats. Same pop-up as the population layer.

layers.name: House seats today (2020 apportionment)
layers.shows: Each state's House seats after the 2020 census.

layers.name: Ratifying the Constitution, 1787–1791
layers.shows: A pie where each state's ratifying convention met: votes to ratify (blue) and against (orange-red), with bigger pies for more delegates. Labels give the state and the order it ratified (DE 1 to VT 14). Each pop-up gives the result, date and vote, where the convention met, and a note. North Carolina has two pies: its first convention, at Hillsborough in 1788 (label NC (1788)), did not ratify.
layers.source: Center for the Study of the American Constitution, University of Wisconsin–Madison (votes, dates and meeting places)

knownIssues.where: Ratifying the Constitution, North Carolina (1788) pie and pop-up
knownIssues.note: Sources disagree on this vote, not a map error. The layer follows its own source, the Center for the Study of the American Constitution's Documentary History of the Ratification: 2 August 1788, 83 for and 184 against. [NCpedia](https://www.ncpedia.org/government/convention-1788) gives 1 August 1788 and 184 to 84. Either way the substance holds: the Hillsborough convention neither ratified nor rejected the Constitution until amendments were considered, as the pop-up's note says.

compellingQuestion.en: How did the Constitution balance large and small states, and how close did it come to being rejected?
compellingQuestion.es: ¿Cómo equilibró la Constitución a los estados grandes y pequeños, y qué tan cerca estuvo de ser rechazada?

questions.task: Open The states in 1790 bookmark. Students compare the pie sizes to find the most populous state, then click the pies and read the 1790 census line of each pop-up to find the states where more than a quarter of the people were enslaved.

student.en: Open The states in 1790 bookmark and click the pies. Which state had the most people? In which states were more than a quarter of the people enslaved? The first line of each pop-up gives the percentage.
student.es: Abre el marcador The states in 1790 (los estados en 1790) y haz clic en los gráficos circulares. ¿Qué estado tenía más habitantes? ¿En qué estados más de una cuarta parte de la población estaba esclavizada? La primera línea de cada ventana emergente da el porcentaje.

answer.where: The states in 1790 bookmark; Population in 1790 layer. Biggest pie and pop-up first line: Virginia, 747,610 people (Kentucky is counted separately; Massachusetts, which then included Maine, is next with 475,327). The percentage in the first line of each pop-up ("1790 census: … people, … of them enslaved (…%)") is above 25 in five states, listed below. Legend: blue = free people, orange-red = enslaved people.

table.caption: States where more than a quarter of the people were enslaved in 1790, from the pop-ups

questions.task: Turn on House seats in 1793. Students use the labels (abbreviation and seats) and the legend to find the states with the most and fewest seats, then read the pop-up to compare House seats with senators.

student.en: In Map layers, turn on House seats in 1793. Each label gives the state and its seats, and darker blue means more seats. Which state had the most seats in the House of Representatives, and which the fewest? Click two states: how many senators did each have? Why do you think the House and the Senate are counted differently?
student.es: En las capas del mapa (Map layers), activa House seats in 1793 (escaños en la Cámara en 1793). Cada etiqueta da el estado y sus escaños, y un azul más oscuro indica más escaños. ¿Qué estado tenía más escaños en la Cámara de Representantes y cuál tenía menos? Haz clic en dos estados: ¿cuántos senadores tenía cada uno? ¿Por qué crees que la Cámara y el Senado se cuentan de forma distinta?

answer.where: House seats in 1793 layer. Labels and legend (darkest class, 13 to 19 seats): Virginia, VA: 19, the most of the 105 seats. Palest class (1 to 2 seats): Delaware, DE: 1, the fewest; Vermont, Rhode Island, Kentucky and Georgia have 2. Pop-up, third line: "plus 2 senators, like every state".
answer.accept: A good answer names Virginia (19) and Delaware (1), says every state had two senators, and explains the Great Compromise in its own words: House seats follow population, which suited the large states, while the equal Senate protected the small ones. The pop-up also gives the ratio, one seat for every 33,000 people counted.

title.es: La cláusula de los tres quintos

questions.task: Students click Virginia and South Carolina and read the last two lines of each pop-up, which give the seats each would have had if enslaved people had been counted in full or not at all, and compare them with the actual seats. Then they look for other states where the two numbers differ.

student.en: Under the three-fifths clause, three of every five enslaved people were counted when House seats were shared out. Click Virginia and South Carolina and read the last two lines of each pop-up: how many seats would each have had if enslaved people had been counted in full, or not at all? Click other states too: which ones gained seats by counting people who could not vote?
student.es: Según la cláusula de los tres quintos, se contaban tres de cada cinco personas esclavizadas al repartir los escaños de la Cámara. Haz clic en Virginia y en Carolina del Sur y lee las dos últimas líneas de cada ventana emergente: ¿cuántos escaños habría tenido cada uno si se hubiera contado a todas las personas esclavizadas, o a ninguna? Haz clic también en otros estados: ¿cuáles ganaron escaños al contar a personas que no podían votar?

fill.en: Virginia: ____ seats with the three-fifths clause; ____ if enslaved people were not counted.
fill.es: Virginia: ____ escaños con la cláusula de los tres quintos; ____ si no se contaba a las personas esclavizadas.

answer.where: Population in 1790 or House seats in 1793 pop-up, the lines "That gave … House seats in 1793", "If enslaved people had been counted in full" and "If they had not been counted at all". Virginia: 19, 22, 13. South Carolina: 6, 7, 4. Seven states show a higher seat count under the clause than with no count, listed below.
answer.accept: A good answer gives Virginia 19 and 13 (fill-in) and South Carolina 6 and 4, names at least Virginia, North Carolina, Maryland and South Carolina as states that gained seats, and says that enslaved people were counted for seats but could not vote, so the gain went to the slaveholding states. The seven states gained 15 seats in all (105 instead of 90), Virginia alone 6.

table.caption: States whose House seats changed with the three-fifths clause, from the pop-ups

questions.task: Turn off Population in 1790 and House seats in 1793 and turn on Ratifying the Constitution. Students click the pies, read the vote line of each pop-up ("Ratified on …: … for, … against") to find the three closest votes, and open both North Carolina pies to explain why there are two.

student.en: Turn off Population in 1790 and House seats in 1793, and turn on Ratifying the Constitution. Click the pies and read the first line of each pop-up, which gives the votes for and against. Which three votes were closest? North Carolina has two pies: click both and explain why.
student.es: Desactiva Population in 1790 y House seats in 1793, y activa Ratifying the Constitution (la ratificación de la Constitución). Haz clic en los gráficos y lee la primera línea de cada ventana emergente, que da los votos a favor y en contra. ¿Qué tres votaciones fueron las más reñidas? Carolina del Norte tiene dos gráficos: haz clic en ambos y explica por qué.

answer.where: Ratifying the Constitution layer; legend: blue = voted to ratify, orange-red = voted against. Pop-up first line: Rhode Island 34 for, 32 against (label RI 13, May 29, 1790); New York 30–27 (NY 11, July 26, 1788); Massachusetts 187–168 (MA 6, February 6, 1788). By number of votes the next closest are Virginia 89–79 (VA 10) and New Hampshire 57–47 (NH 9, the ninth state, enough to put the Constitution into effect). North Carolina: the NC (1788) pie at Hillsborough, titled "Did not ratify (first convention)", 83 for, 184 against, with a note that a second convention ratified in November 1789; the NC 12 pie at Fayetteville, 194–77, November 21, 1789.
answer.accept: A good answer names Rhode Island, New York and Massachusetts (accept Virginia or New Hampshire if the student counts the gap in votes rather than the share), and explains that North Carolina's first convention did not ratify and a second one did more than a year later, after Congress had proposed the Bill of Rights. Sources differ on the exact 1788 vote and date; accept the pop-up's figures.

final.teacher: Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph; sketch pins for James Madison, Alexander Hamilton, Patrick Henry and George Mason, each with a quote and the principle it argues about (sketches are not saved, so finish in one session or take a screenshot); or a short talk using the map.

student.en: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.
student.es: Responde la pregunta central con evidencia de al menos dos capas del mapa. Puedes escribir un párrafo, dibujar en el mapa o hacer ambas cosas.

objectives: Compare the pie sizes in the Population in 1790 layer to find the most populous state, and read the census line of the pop-ups to identify the states where more than a quarter of the people were enslaved.
Use the labels and legend of the House seats in 1793 layer to find the states with the most and fewest House seats, and compare each state's House seats with its two senators.
Read the Virginia and South Carolina pop-ups to compare the seats each actually had with the seats it would have had if enslaved people had been counted in full or not at all.
Read the vote line in the Ratifying the Constitution pop-ups to find the three closest ratification votes and explain why North Carolina has two pies.
Use population and seat figures from at least two states as evidence for how the three-fifths clause shifted power in the House.
discussion: Virginia had the most people and the most House seats but the same two senators as Delaware. Looking at the pies and the seat labels, which states had most to gain from each half of that bargain?

Compare the actual seats for Virginia and South Carolina with the two alternatives in their pop-ups. How many seats did the three-fifths clause move, and who in those states did that extra representation speak for?
The closest ratification votes were in some of the biggest states, and North Carolina voted twice. What does the map suggest might have happened if one or two of those votes had gone the other way?

resources.title: Constitution of the United States: A History
History of the U.S. Census Bureau: 1790 Overview

beforeYouStart.en: In 1787, delegates from twelve states met in Philadelphia and wrote the Constitution. Large and small states disagreed about how many votes each should have in Congress. The Constitution would take effect only when nine states had ratified it, each at a special convention.
beforeYouStart.es: En 1787, delegados de doce estados se reunieron en Filadelfia y redactaron la Constitución. Los estados grandes y los pequeños no estaban de acuerdo sobre cuántos votos debía tener cada uno en el Congreso. La Constitución solo entraría en vigor cuando nueve estados la ratificaran, cada uno en una convención especial.

readingTheMap.en: The map has no place names: click a pie or a state to see its name in the pop-up title. Pies on the states show the people in 1790: blue for free, orange-red for enslaved, and bigger pies for more people. Three layers are off when the map opens. In House seats in 1793, darker blue means more seats, and each label gives the state's abbreviation and seats. In Ratifying the Constitution, each pie sits where a state's convention met: blue for votes to ratify, orange-red for votes against, and labels give the order each state ratified. Maine is shown within Massachusetts and West Virginia within Virginia.
readingTheMap.es: El mapa no tiene nombres de lugares: haz clic en un gráfico circular o en un estado para ver su nombre en el título de la ventana emergente. Los gráficos sobre los estados muestran la población en 1790: azul para las personas libres, rojo anaranjado para las esclavizadas, y los gráficos más grandes indican más habitantes. Tres capas están desactivadas al abrir el mapa. En House seats in 1793, un azul más oscuro indica más escaños, y cada etiqueta da la abreviatura del estado y sus escaños. En Ratifying the Constitution, cada gráfico está donde se reunió la convención de un estado: azul para los votos a favor de ratificar, rojo anaranjado para los votos en contra, y las etiquetas indican el orden en que ratificó cada estado. Maine aparece dentro de Massachusetts y Virginia Occidental dentro de Virginia.

reflection.en: What did the map show you about the Constitution that you might not have noticed from reading alone?
reflection.es: ¿Qué te mostró el mapa sobre la Constitución que quizá no habrías notado solo con la lectura?

teacherNotes.beforeClass: Open the map and check it loads. House seats in 1793, House seats today and Ratifying the Constitution are off at the start; the basemap has no place names, so students click for a state's name. Download the student sheet. Share the map with the Google Classroom button (it shares the map only; attach the sheet separately). No account or login is needed; sketches are not saved. Read the answers on the teacher page.

misconceptions.claim: The three-fifths clause gave enslaved people a share of representation.
misconceptions.response: It gave slaveholding states more seats, not enslaved people a voice: they could not vote. Virginia's pop-up shows 19 seats under the clause, against 13 if enslaved people had not been counted.

misconceptions.claim: Every state ratified the Constitution easily.
misconceptions.response: Rhode Island ratified by 34 to 32 and New York by 30 to 27, and North Carolina's first convention did not ratify.
Every state had two senators; only House seats followed population.

standards.text: Analyze the issues of the Constitutional Convention of 1787, including the Great Compromise and the Three-Fifths Compromise

Analyze the arguments of the Federalists and Anti-Federalists, including those of Alexander Hamilton, Patrick Henry, James Madison, and George Mason, and explain how their debates exemplify civil discourse

Examine the course and consequences of the Constitutional Convention (New Jersey Plan, Virginia Plan, Great Compromise, Three-Fifths Compromise, compromises regarding taxation and slave trade, Electoral College, state vs. federal power, empowering a president).
Analyze support and opposition (Federalists, Federalist Papers, Anti-Federalists, Bill of Rights) to ratification of the U.S. Constitution.
Explain the origins, functions, and structure of government with reference to the U.S. Constitution, state constitutions, and selected other systems of government.
Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics.
